transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-22
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Carlos Vega (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Atlas CTO), Ethan Park (Head of ML), Liam O'Neill (DevOps)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery focused on reserved GPU sizing, tenant isolation (per-team vs per-customer pools), prewarm strategies for teleop bursts, potential fallback to Redwood hosted in outages, and security/audit requirements. Agreed next steps and PoC scope.

[00:00] Carlos: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on — I'm Carlos from Redwood, AE on the account, this is Priya our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Maya: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to dig in.
[00:11] Ethan: Yeah thanks — we wanted to make sure we cover our burst pattern and multi-tenant needs.
[00:16] Priya: Great, quick note I'll be the technical lead here and will ask a bunch of follow ups around traffic shape and isolation.
[00:24] Carlos: Quick agenda — understand your workloads, isolation requirements, prewarm/warm pool expectations, fallback strategy, and security/compliance. Then next steps. Sound ok?
[00:31] Maya: Yep. We'll start with context. Atlas Robotics runs fleets of warehouse robots and teleoperation sessions. We do on-device pre-processing but heavy language models run in the cloud for high-level instruction decoding and natural language teleop support. Latency spikes during operator handoffs and shipping windows, short bursts but high qps.
[00:50] Ethan: Exactly — typical background inference is low (like 50-100 qps) but every 30-60 minutes we have 30s-2min bursts where qps multiplies by 8-12x depending on region. That's what scares us with dedicated capacity.
[01:10] Priya: Do you have a histogram or sliding window counts for tokens/sec or requests/sec? That helps pick reserved GPU count and warm pool sizes.
[01:18] Ethan: We can produce a 7-day histogram — I think we can share it this week. We'll include distribution by customer and by team.
[01:26] Liam: From infra side, we need isolation — some enterprise customers require tenancy isolation at physical node level. So multi-tenant on same GPU is not always acceptable. We were thinking of mixing per-tenant pools and a shared overflow pool.
[01:40] Carlos: Good — so two constraints: strong isolation for certain customers plus a cost-sensitive baseline pool. Redwood Dedicated supports node-level isolation (segregated nodes) and also warm pools for prewarming. Priya i'll hand off to you for details on sizing and prewarm behavior.
[01:55] Priya: Thanks — two main levers for us: reserved GPU count and warm-pool size/config, and the prewarm prefill policy (keep KV cache warmed for last-k requests or maintain hot processes). For your burst characteristics, I'd recommend a mix: allocate segregated nodes for the top X enterprise customers, reserve a baseline shared pool for steady-state traffic, and a warm pool that can prewarm replicas for the overflow workload.
[02:20] Maya: When you say warm pool, how fast can those replicas become ready? We need <200ms additional latency for operator sessions, otherwise the UX degrades.
[02:28] Priya: Warm pool velocity depends on model size and GPU type. For a 30B-ish model on A100/RTX, warm pool can often service new requests in ~500ms - 2s depending on whether KV cache is required. For strict <200ms, you'd need more pinned capacity or prewarmed KV caches per session. We can also leverage lightweight distillation models for fast fallbacks.
[02:50] Ethan: Hmm — we tried small local models but they lose fidelity on complex instructions. Fallback quality matters.
[02:57] Priya: Understood. There's an architectural option: keep a small number of hot replicas per region pinned to high-priority tenants (pinned instances), and route lower-priority bursts to warm pool with slightly higher latency. That means slightly higher cost but preserves UX for your paying customers.
[03:15] Carlos: Also worth considering dynamic routing policy: route by SLO tier — gold customers to pinned nodes, silver to warm pool, bronze to hosted fallback. Does that map to your billing tiers?
[03:26] Maya: Yes that's close. Some customers require SOC2 and physical isolation — that's gold. Others are fine with logical isolation.
[03:33] Liam: On networking — we need to know VPC peering options. We are likely to use Redwood Private (VPC) for the segregated nodes, but want an option to failover to Redwood hosted in a cross-region outage. How do you do failover while preserving keys and logs?
[03:47] Priya: For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for keys. Audit logs can be exported to your SIEM. Failover to hosted requires replication of model artifacts and an agreed fallback routing policy. We can configure automatic fallback to a hosted variant or reduced-size model variant if your Private cluster is degraded. Key rotation and data residency need to be planned — we typically use envelope encryption so secrets stay in your KMS.
[04:10] Ethan: What's the time to spin up a full Private node in another region? We can't rely on cold provisioning during incidents.
[04:16] Priya: Cold provisioning can be minutes to hours depending on cloud quotas. That's why we recommend reserved capacity in target region or a cross-region warm pool. Alternatively, pre-provision minimal standby capacity or enable burst capacity with advance reservations.
[04:30] Carlos: Just to flag pricing — reserved nodes + warm pools increase cost but give predictable latency. We'll send a tiered pricing spreadsheet illustrating tradeoffs.
[04:40] Maya: Good. A couple of specific questions: 1) isolation down to GPU boundary? 2) how do you handle model updates and KV cache invalidation without disruption? And 3) can we enforce per-customer audit retention windows?
[04:54] Priya: 1) Yes we support placement policies that pin tenants to physical GPUs or to dedicated pods. 2) For model updates we do canary rollouts and maintain compatibility layer for KV caches — if model changes break cache semantics we invalidate per-route caches and prewarm new caches as part of rollout. 3) Audit retention is configurable; we can export logs to your storage with retention policies per customer — though retention segmentation sometimes needs legal/contract adjustments.
[05:22] Liam: For the canary process, can we run local canaries in our Private cluster before cutting the live route? We want to test outputs on internal prompts.
[05:30] Priya: Absolutely — Private supports staged rollouts and you can run canaries against a subset of traffic or internal test harness. We also support a feature flagging mechanism to route test tokens.
[05:38] Ethan: For sizing — if we wanted to be able to sustain a 10x burst every hour for up to 2 minutes across three regions, what are the right questions we should answer?
[05:47] Priya: We'll need: baseline QPS, peak QPS per region, typical sequence length (tokens per request), concurrency per session, percent of requests that need KV cache warm vs stateless, and topology of which tenants require isolation. If you can provide a 7-day histogram, we can propose a starting reserved pool and warm pool numbers.
[06:05] Ethan: Ok we'll collect that. For the PoC, we'd like Redwood to run a synthetic replay of our burst profile and measure p95 latency and token cost. Is that doable?
[06:13] Priya: Yes — we'll propose a PoC benchmark plan. Usually SE runs a replay in a staging environment or on a dedicated cluster with instrumented tracing. We can measure cold vs warm vs hot latency and give recommendations on how many pinned replicas are needed.
[06:25] Carlos: Quick commercial note — reserved capacity can be monthly or annual commit. Also there's a burst allowance for short spikes if you buy a warm-pool configuration.
[06:34] Maya: Good to know. Security — SOC2 type II is a hard requirement for some customers. Do you have that?
[06:40] Carlos: Redwood is SOC2 TYPE II certified — we can share the cert and our compliance pack. We'll attach it in the follow up.
[06:47] Maya: Great. And SSO? We use Okta and SCIM provisioning.
[06:50] Priya: We support SAML/SSO and SCIM for user provisioning, and RBAC is configurable per workspace and per route.
[06:58] Liam: One more infra ask — do you support GPU partitioning (MIG-like) for cost efficiency? Some of our non-critical workloads could run on fractional GPUs.
[07:08] Priya: We support fractionalization on specific hardware types where available, and multi-tenant scheduling with memory isolation, but for strict physical isolation we recommend full-device pinning. We'll clarify supported GPU families in the follow up.
[07:22] Ethan: Competitors question — we've looked at SageMaker endpoints and some boutique inference providers. Why Redwood vs those?
[07:30] Carlos: Short answer: production-first tooling and predictable unit economics across hosted/dedicated/private, plus fine-grained routing and built-in observability for token-level cost. Priya can add details on performance tuning.
[07:42] Priya: We also optimize kernel paths, batching, and KV caching to reduce per-token cost while preserving latency. For example, dynamic batching windows tuned to your sequence length profile often cut costs substantially.
[07:55] Maya: Sounds promising. Let's get into a few hypothetical numbers to see tradeoffs. If we need to guarantee <200ms p95 for gold tenants during bursts, what's the rough reserved GPU count for a 30B model?
[08:08] Priya: Rough back-of-envelope: depends on model throughput on chosen GPU. On A100 a 30B can do ~20-40 tokens/sec per replica depending on optimization; but p95 <200ms typically requires a - sorry this is fuzzy in the transcript - it typically requires enough hot replicas to serve concurrent sessions without queueing. We'll run numbers in the follow-up spreadsheet.
[08:30] Ethan: Understood — we can take model size and target session concurrency to you.
[08:34] Carlos: Next steps recap: Carlos will send pricing and prewarm design doc; Priya will send PoC benchmark plan; Atlas will provide traffic histograms, sample prompts, and VPC/KMS details. Then schedule PoC kickoff.
[08:46] Maya: That works. Anything else on compliance?
[08:49] Carlos: We'll also include our SOC2 packet and a note on encryption in transit and at rest.
[08:55] Liam: One small note — our procurement team prefers contract language around failover SLAs and data deletion guarantees. We'll surface that after internal review.
[09:04] Carlos: Thank you — we'll include a procurement checklist in the follow up.
[09:09] Priya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with dates.
[09:12] Maya: Thanks. Bye.

(occasional minor speaker label mismatches and filler words in transcript, auto-transcription errors: e.g., 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cape', 'prewarm' as 'pre warm')
recording_notes: Call ran 49 minutes; medium transcription quality; several technical follow-ups assigned. Customer emphasized operator UX and <200ms p95 need for gold tenants; agreed to provide traffic histograms and sample prompts for PoC.
